transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-10-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Erin Patel (Nimbus CTO), Marcus Green (Nimbus SRE), Sofia Alvarez (Nimbus ML)

Summary: quick console walkthrough focusing on tracing, error analysis, and request logs for debugging flows. Customer cares about end-to-end request observability, ability to tie failures to model versions, and privacy/redaction controls for logs.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro - I'm Alex, AE on the account, priya and Jordan from engineering will do most of the demo. Erin, Marcus, Sofia, thanks for making time.
[00:20] Erin Patel: Thanks Alex. Quick note, we got the invite - Marcus is our SRE, Sofia handles ML infra, I'm here for prioritization and timelines.
[00:35] Priya Rao: Great. Today we'll walk the Redwood Console tracing view, error analysis, and request logs. We'll show how you can jump from a high-level error spike down to the raw request and backtrace into the model variant.
[01:05] Marcus Green: Top concerns for us: can we correlate latency spikes with model changes, and how private are the request logs? We have strict PCI-ish requirements, we need redaction or KMS control.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: Totally. We'll cover KMS integration, audit logs, and how to configure redaction and retention. Also show how tracing ties into rollout policies so you can roll back quickly.
[02:10] Priya Rao: Opening console - landing page shows per-route token throughput and latency. We'll click into the chat-gen route. You'll see a timeline with traces and an error rate panel.
[02:35] [sound of screen share notification]
[03:00] Priya Rao: Here you can see a spike at 09:12 UTC yesterday. Click trace list. Each trace is sampled; we support configurable sampling rates and head-based capture for errors. Note: sampling setting is per-route and per-environment.
[03:40] Erin Patel: How long do traces keep, and can we export them?
[03:50] Jordan Lee: Retention is configurable by plan; you can export JSONL of traces or ship to your SIEM. For Private deployments you control retention in your VPC. Exports can be filtered by model version, route, or request ID.
[04:15] Priya Rao: Here's a single trace. You see spans: API gateway, routing, tokenization, model exec, kv-cache lookup - sometimes the transcript generator shows KV "cash" in logs due to ASR but that's just a transcription thing.
[04:45] Marcus Green: Can we see environment tags? Like commit sha or model-version label?
[04:55] Priya Rao: Yep - every trace includes metadata: model_version, node_id, container_id, and a user-provided rollout tag. You can search traces by model_version or rollout tag to correlate regressions.
[05:25] Sofia Alvarez: If a model roll out caused regressions, can we automatically route traffic back to previous variant?
[05:35] Jordan Lee: Yes, Redwood supports automatic fallback: policy-driven routing back to pinned model_version or a cheaper latency-tier when errors exceed threshold. Demo later.
[06:00] [06:00] Erin Patel: On privacy: we can't persist raw PII. How do you support redaction?
[06:10] Priya Rao: Two layers: client-side redaction via SDK hooks (recommended) and server-side redaction rules in the console (regex/field rules). For sensitive tokens we also support envelope encryption with customer KMS so logs are encrypted-at-rest with your keys.
[06:45] Marcus Green: Great. Do audit logs show who accessed which request logs? We need full audit trail.
[06:55] Jordan Lee: Yes, audit logs show user, IP, action, and object. They are exportable and immutable for the configured retention window.
[07:20] Priya Rao: Back to trace view - error analysis panel aggregates top error messages and groups by stack trace and model_version. It will surface repeated causes like timeouts, tokenization errors, or policy rejections.
[07:55] [07:55] Sofia Alvarez: Can I get example regex for PII redaction?
[08:05] Priya Rao: We'll send a doc with examples - email follow-up.
[08:20] Priya Rao: Now request logs: this is the raw request/response capture. We show latency, tokens in/out, policy filter flags, and a small snippet of the generated text (which is redacted by default for enterprise accounts).
[08:50] Marcus Green: If we need to debug a specific user issue, how do we tie from customer ticket to request log? We track request_id?
[09:00] Priya Rao: Every request includes a UUID request_id. You can search by request_id, user_id (if you forward it), or session tags. We also support instrumentation to add your correlation-id header.
[09:30] [09:30] Erin Patel: About performance: we lose throughput sometimes - is there a way to see kernel-level or GPU-level slowdown?
[09:40] Jordan Lee: For Dedicated pools we surface node-level metrics like GPU utilization, mem pressure, and per-node qps. Our tracing spans include model exec time broken down into attention, kv-cache lookup, and decode. It won't show CUDA kernel names in the Console but you can export traces and we can correlate with host-level telemetry if you push metrics to our observability integration.
[10:20] Priya Rao: Here's an error trace where model exec time suddenly increases because of long prefix replays - we surface prefix length in the trace. We can show recommendations: enable prefix caching or increase batch size for similar requests.
[10:55] Marcus Green: That sounds useful. Is there automated guidance?
[11:00] Priya Rao: Yes, in Redwood Optimize we run analysis over traces and workloads and provide recommended batching and quantization settings - we'll share Optimize outputs as part of the pilot.
[11:30] [11:30] Sofia Alvarez: We use a mix of short chat and long doc summarization flows. Will the tracing and request logs mix these together?
[11:40] Jordan Lee: You can filter by route and by prompt length; the console also tags short vs long flows. We recommend separate routes for long-running summarization so you can set different SLOs and batching rules.
[12:05] Priya Rao: Switching to error analysis dashboard - top errors are timeouts, policy rejections, and unexpected null outputs. You can click into the "null outputs" bucket and see a sample distribution by model_version.
[12:40] Erin Patel: What about reproducibility - can we re-run a request against another model or exact model_version?
[12:50] Priya Rao: Yes, we have replay tooling: you can replay a single request against a pinned model_version in an isolated sandbox. We also provide a compare view to diff outputs. Note: replaying may expose data so replays are gated to users with proper permissions.
[13:20] Marcus Green: Permissions - RBAC?
[13:25] Jordan Lee: RBAC, SAML/SSO, and org-level roles. You can set role that denies access to raw request payloads while allowing metrics and aggregated traces.
[13:50] [13:50] Sofia Alvarez: For debugging, we often need raw tokens and KV cache states. Can we capture KV cache snapshots?
[13:58] Priya Rao: We capture KV cache hits/misses stats and prefix match lengths; full KV snapshots are sensitive but for Private deployments we can enable deeper capture under strict access controls. We'll document the tradeoffs.
[14:30] Priya Rao: Now demoing a debugging flow - we search for an error spike, pick a failing trace, jump to the request log entry and copy request_id. Then we open the replay panel.
[15:05] [15:05] screen noise
[15:20] Priya Rao: Replaying against previous model_version shows the failure disappears - indicates a model regression. We then use rollout controls to rollback traffic to previous variant.
[15:50] Erin Patel: How quick is rollback?
[15:55] Jordan Lee: Rollbacks are immediate for new requests; in-flight requests will finish on their existing variant. You can do canary rollouts and specify health checks like error-rate thresholds or median latency.
[16:25] Marcus Green: Is there a throttling or circuit breaker?
[16:30] Priya Rao: Yes, circuit breaker that can drop to cached responses or pin to a lower-cost variant. Also traffic shaping to limit QPS per-user/session.
[17:00] [17:00] Sofia Alvarez: I saw "policy rejections" - is that the content policy or our internal rules?
[17:08] Jordan Lee: Mostly content policy checks at the API edge; you can add custom policy hooks or filter at the route level and tag those as "policy_reject" in traces.
[17:45] Priya Rao: Jumping to request-logs export - you can export matching queries to S3 or our logging integration. For PCI compliance we recommend using your own S3 encryption + KMS so logs never live in Redwood-managed storage unencrypted by your keys.
[18:10] Marcus Green: Nice. For the pilot we need a small Dedicated pool. What's the typical lead time?
[18:20] Alex Chen: For Dedicated it's usually 2-4 weeks depending on capacity and region. We'll start sizing after Priya runs the lightweight benchmark.
[18:40] [18:40] Erin Patel: Any gotchas with VPC/on-prem? We have a strict networking policy.
[18:50] Jordan Lee: For VPC Private deployments we provide a control plane that talks to your VPC via peering or private link. For on-prem we have an installer and the control plane can be air-gapped if needed. We'll share the private deployment checklist.
[19:25] Priya Rao: Demoing trace filters: we filter by model_version=2027-09-30-experiment, error_type=timeout, and we get distribution across nodes. You can create alerts off this query.
[20:00] Marcus Green: Are alerts integrated with PagerDuty or Slack?
[20:05] Jordan Lee: Yes, webhook, PagerDuty, Slack, and export to CloudWatch.
[20:25] [20:25] Priya Rao: Now the error analysis timeline - click a sample error cluster, it shows top contributing routes and an example request. You can open that request in the live debug view and step through token-by-token latency.
[21:00] Sofia Alvarez: Token-by-token tracing, interesting. We worry about long-tail latency on decode steps.
[21:10] Priya Rao: The trace will show per-token decode time and indicates if the slow token is due to model attention or IO.
[21:40] Alex Chen: Quick question from pricing - if we increase sampling for traces to 100%, does that impact bill?
[21:50] Jordan Lee: Trace storage and export bandwidth are billed; we recommend targeted 100% for short windows during incidents. Sampling costs are modest compared to tokens but we'll include a sample cost estimate in the pricing doc.
[22:20] [22:20] Marcus Green: For compliance we'll probably request end-to-end proofs for SOC2. Do you provide SOC2 + pen test reports?
[22:30] Alex Chen: Yes, SOC2 Type II, and we can share redacted reports under NDA. We'll attach security pack in follow-up.
[22:50] Priya Rao: Wrapping up console features - also available: per-route latency percentiles, token-level cost breakdown, and per-model regression alerts linked to eval test sets.
[23:20] Sofia Alvarez: Do you integrate with our internal eval framework?
[23:30] Jordan Lee: We can ingest eval artifacts and connect alerts to specific evaluation prompts so regressions trigger only if eval score drops.
[23:55] [23:55] Priya Rao: Final demo: show request-log search using correlation-id header - searching returned 17 matches, we opened the earliest and traced back to a model weight change that matches your release timestamp.
[24:30] Erin Patel: That was the confirm I needed. If the regression is in the model, we'll want to roll back automatically.
[24:40] Priya Rao: We'll set up the policy to monitor 5xx rate and median latency per-route and automatically revert on breach.
[25:00] Marcus Green: For the pilot should we give you full traffic or sampled traffic?
[25:05] Alex Chen: Start with a mirrored sampled stream - mirror 10% of traffic to Redwood Dedicated so you can validate behavior without impacting production. Then ramp up after success criteria are met.
[25:30] [25:30] Sofia Alvarez: About replay security - who can run replays?
[25:35] Jordan Lee: Replay permission is gated; we can create a role that only a handful of engineers have. Replays are logged in audit trail.
[26:00] Priya Rao: Quick note: sometimes transcripts or automated ASR will garble product terms - e.g., KV cache -> KV cash, or we might have "prefix cache" spelled odd. Ignore those in the transcript, console shows accurate names.
[26:25] Erin Patel: Good to know.
[26:40] [26:40] Priya Rao: Any other questions?
[26:45] Marcus Green: One more: how do we get latency breakdown per-customer? We need multi-tenant reporting.
[26:55] Jordan Lee: Per-customer or per-API-key reporting is supported; you'll see per-tenant percentiles and you can slice charts by API key.
[27:20] Priya Rao: Demo closing - we'll attach the recording and the console deck.
[27:35] Alex Chen: Next steps recap: I'll send pricing and SLA, Priya will run a 24h trace/bench, Marcus will provide request IDs and redaction requirements, Sofia will confirm eval integration. We'll tentatively schedule pilot kickoff for 2027-10-18.
[28:00] Erin Patel: Sounds good. Any blockers on our end? Marcus: we need to check firewall rules.
[28:10] Marcus Green: Yeah, we'll share networking contact info after this call.
[28:25] Priya Rao: Great. We'll follow up with the security pack and private-deployment checklist.
[28:40] Alex Chen: Thanks everyone - we'll send notes and action items.
[28:50] [crosstalk] Erin Patel: Thanks all.
[29:00] [meeting ends - rest of 23 minutes used for post-demo Q&A and sign-off recorded in meeting notes - truncated for brevity]

Notes: Transcript contains some ASR errors and occasional speaker mis-attribution. Exported file includes links: "Console Deck" (https://redwood.ai/decks/console-tracing), "Security Pack" (link sent via email), and sample benchmark spreadsheet (to be shared by Priya).
